answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Reeve is credited with this line everywhere — including on the homepage of the Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation ↗, the organisation he founded. But no book page, speech, interview or letter documents this exact wording. The closest sentence anyone can actually source, from his 2002 book Nothing Is Impossible, runs “Once we choose hope, everything is possible” — the same thought, not the same words.
answer.confidenceText: Credited to Reeve by his own foundation and consistent with everything he wrote — but the exact wording is sourced to nothing.

source.excerpt: Once you choose hope, anything’s possible.
trail: Reeve’s own foundation leads with the line. The homepage of the Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation ↗ displays “Once you choose hope, anything’s possible.” — with no source date attached. That is institutional endorsement, not a citation.

Wikiquote doesn’t carry it at all. The Christopher Reeve page on Wikiquote ↗ contains no “once you choose hope” entry in any section — though it does source his 1996 Democratic National Convention line about dreams that “at first seem impossible.”

The closest documented sentence is in the 2002 book. LibQuotes ↗ reproduces a passage ending “Once we choose hope, everything is possible,” citing Nothing Is Impossible: Reflections on a New Life (Random House, 2002).

The Reeve archive lists the short form undated. CapedWonder ↗ carries “Once you choose hope, anything’s possible” with no date, while separately sourcing the “lighthouse is hope” passage to Nothing is Impossible (2002) — a telling split.
source.excerptNote: This is the form that circulates, and the form Reeve’s own foundation uses. The sentence that is documented — in the closing chapter of Nothing Is Impossible, titled “Hope” — is a different one: “Once we choose hope, everything is possible.” Two pronouns and one adjective apart, and no citation bridges them.

source.rightsNote: We could not pin this exact wording to a specific work, but that does not make it free to reuse: Christopher Reeve died in 2004, and every candidate source — Still Me (1998), Nothing Is Impossible (2002), his speeches and interviews — is a modern work published well after 1931 and firmly in copyright. Treat the line as in-copyright and quote it with attribution.

author.name: Christopher Reeve
author.heading: Who was Christopher Reeve?
author.bio: Christopher Reeve (25 September 1952 – 10 October 2004) was the American actor who defined Superman on screen across four films, and who in May 1995 was thrown from a horse and left paralysed from the neck down. He spent the nine years that followed as the most visible advocate for spinal-cord-injury research in the world, founding what is now the Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation and co-founding the Reeve-Irvine Research Center. He wrote two books about that second life — Still Me (1998) and Nothing Is Impossible: Reflections on a New Life (2002) — and directed for television from a wheelchair. The line about choosing hope is credited to him because it is precisely what he spent a decade arguing, in print and from podiums; the irony is that the version the world memorised is not quite the version he published.

cite.sourceCitation: No source documents the popular wording. Closest documented: Christopher Reeve, Nothing Is Impossible: Reflections on a New Life (New York: Random House, 2002), closing chapter “Hope” — “Once we choose hope, everything is possible.”

misattribution.heading: The wording, not the man
misattribution.intro: Nobody is stealing this line from Reeve — the attribution to him is almost certainly right. What has gone soft is the wording, and the confident sourcing that quote sites bolt onto it.

items.why: The passage that can be cited to a book ends: “Once we choose hope, everything is possible.” LibQuotes ↗ attributes it to Nothing Is Impossible (Random House, 2002), and CapedWonder ↗ independently sources the same passage to that book.
The popular form appears on his foundation’s homepage ↗ and across every quote aggregator — but always bare. Goodreads ↗ gives the name and a “hope” tag and nothing else: no book, no page, no date.

Search engines and quote pages routinely assign the short line to the 2002 book. No source we could fetch gives a page for it, and the book sentence they point to is worded differently — so this is an inference being passed off as a citation. The Internet Archive copy ↗ is access-restricted, so the text cannot be searched to settle it.
Both forms circulate freely. The contracted version is the one Reeve’s own foundation ↗ prints, which makes it the better default of the two.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is unmistakably Reeve’s, and his family’s foundation stands behind these exact words — but the words themselves are the one thing nobody can source. Quote it as attributed, and if you need a sentence you can cite to a page, use the book’s: “Once we choose hope, everything is possible” (Nothing Is Impossible, 2002 ↗).

context.heading: Why this one is different
lead: Most feel-good lines pinned on famous names are drifting away from their source. This one is drifting within it. Reeve wrote an entire closing chapter called “Hope” for Nothing Is Impossible, published in September 2002 — seven years after the 1995 riding accident that left him paralysed from the neck down. The book is saturated with this exact argument. The problem isn’t whether he believed it; it’s that the sentence everyone quotes isn’t the sentence he printed.

What makes the case unusual is the endorsement. The Christopher & Dana Reeve Foundation ↗ — founded by Reeve, carried on by his family — puts the popular wording on its front page. That’s about as close to an authorised text as an unsourced quote ever gets. It still isn’t a citation, and we won’t pretend otherwise.
detailsBody: The verb matters more than it looks. “Choose” is the whole argument: Reeve’s claim was that hope is not a mood that arrives but a decision you make, and that the decision comes first and the possibility second. Both versions of the line carry that; the drift is only in pronoun and scale.

Wikiquote ↗ does source a related and firmly documented Reeve line, from his speech to the Democratic National Convention on 26 August 1996: “So many of our dreams at first seem impossible, then they seem improbable, and then, when we summon the will, they soon become inevitable.” If you want a Reeve sentence on hope with a date and a podium attached, that is the one.
context.pull: Reeve’s foundation prints these exact words. His book prints different ones. Nothing bridges the gap.
